newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl seeks to boost flagging Irish peace process.
newsitem.headline: Kohl seeks to boost flagging Irish peace process.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl sought on Tuesday to boost the flagging Northern Ireland peace process on the eve of a visit to Dublin.

Accompanying Irish President Mary Robinson to the opening of the world's largest book fair in Frankfurt, he said: "We Germans hope with all our hearts that the peace process in Northern Ireland keeps up good progress despite all the obstacles."

Robinson, echoing Kohl's conciliatory tone, took the opportunity to extend a hand of friendship to Protestant Unionists in Northern Ireland who fervently want to maintain the province's links with Britain.

Kohl's two-day visit to Dublin will end on Thursday, the anniversary of Germany's 1990 reunification. He will host a Unity Day reception in the Irish capital to mark the first national day he has spent abroad since the east-west merger.

The chancellor was in reflective mood at the opening of the Frankfurt Book Fair, which takes as its theme this year "Ireland and Its Diaspora" -- the 78 million exiles of Irish descent scattered around the globe from Sydney to New York.

Earlier on Tuesday in Bonn, Kohl presented his memoirs about the 1989-1990 German unification process. In that book, and in his remarks in Frankfurt, the chancellor singled out for particular praise former Irish prime minister Charles Haughey.

"Haughey spoke out without any ifs or buts on the right of Germans to live in an undivided country. For that I want to thank Ireland once again from the bottom of my heart," he said at the opening of the 110-nation book fair.
Kohl is to visit Dublin at a time when the peace process in British-ruled Northern Ireland is fast deteriorating.
Jailed Protestant guerrrillas, a crucial influence in maintaining a two-year truce by Loyalist gunmen who support British links, said they had lost confidence in the peace negotiations.

A 17-month truce by Irish Republican Army guerrillas fighting for Irish unity was shattered in February when they relaunched their bombing campaign on the British mainland. All-party peace talks are bogged down in procedural wrangling.
President Robinson, who as constitutional head of state has to steer clear of commenting on politics, stressed in her speech that "Irishness is simply not territorial".
She urged the Irish to honour and listen to "those whose sense of identity and whose cultural values may be more British than Irish.
"If this is done generously, they too -- the Unionist community -- while affirming their Britishness, might find it easier to acknowledge within themselves a component of Irishness."
Ireland's Nobel prizewinning poet Seamus Heaney hailed Irish exiles from James Joyce to Edna O'Brien who have spread their culture across so many frontiers.
"Displacement, it would seem, is our destiny ... Eden is somewhere we are meant to leave," he said.
